text: Three years I've been volunteering at a drop-in centre for refugee families, and for most of that time I've watched the same thing happen every week: people come in with letters about housing or benefits that they can't untangle, we do our best, and mostly we end up telling them to ring an agency that has a six-week wait. So I put together a proposal for a proper weekly advice clinic with a paid sessional caseworker, someone who actually knows the system. I costed it, I did it properly. The treasurer has now told me, off the record, that the committee would only go for a monthly session, no paid staff, anything complicated referred out — which is basically what we already do, plus a queue. The two women who run intake with me have said if I table that version they'll take it as me selling out the families, because it'll raise hopes and end with people being handed a leaflet. And I get it, I do, but what I can't get past is that the full version has zero chance. None. The money isn't there and nobody on the committee is fighting for it. So my choice is a watered-down thing that at least exists, that maybe in a year I can point at and say look, it's oversubscribed every month, fund it properly — or nothing, just the proposal sitting in my drawer keeping its purity while actual families keep leaving with nothing. My intake colleagues talk like the monthly version kills the real clinic forever, but as far as I can see the real clinic was never alive to kill. There's no deadline, nobody's forcing me to table it this month, but also nobody's coming to rescue this. Am I being naive thinking a foot in the door is worth something, or are they being precious about a plan that was never going to happen? Do I table it?

Portfolio day is Friday and I've been awake since 4am over it, which is daft because I've basically decided.

Background: I'm one of four letting agents at a small branch. Every spring the manager sets the portfolios — which blocks and landlords each of us carries, and the commission attached. She has a fixed habit of rubber-stamping whatever three of the four of us bring her. She doesn't want to arbitrate between us, she wants one sheet with three names on it.

There's a block everyone dreads — huge repair backlog, a landlord who fights every single invoice, tenants churning every few months. Whoever holds it loses their weekends and a decent chunk of their earnings. On Monday two of the others came to me with a split that finally gives me the portfolio I've been angling for since I started — decent blocks, sane landlords, proper money. The price is the nightmare block goes to Anika, the newest agent, for the whole of next year.

The bit I keep circling: Anika pulled me aside yesterday and asked me, face to face, to argue for a fairer share for her at Friday's meeting. She's six months in, she has no idea how the three-names thing works, and I trained her, so I'm the one she came to. I told her I'd see what I could do.

The two colleagues aren't villains but this offer doesn't come round twice. If I walk into that meeting and start fighting Anika's corner, the split is dead, I'm back on the dross for another year, and the only two people who can ever deliver me a majority stop bringing me anything. Somebody has to carry that block, that's just maths. New agents get the rough portfolios everywhere — I did, it's how you learn the job.

So do I just say yes on Friday and keep my mouth shut? I keep picturing her face when the sheet goes up. Tell me this is normal and I've done nothing wrong — or tell me what I'm actually meant to do instead that doesn't cost me the next year of my life.

Meeting's Friday. Three of us bring the manager our portfolio split and she signs whatever has three names on it — that's the system here. This split finally gets me the blocks I've wanted for two years. The catch: the branch's worst block (repair backlog, landlord who fights every invoice, tenants constantly churning) lands on Anika, the new starter, for the next year.

She took me aside yesterday and asked me personally to argue for a fairer share for her. I said I'd see what I could do. Then I took the deal.

She'll see it on the sheet in front of everyone. Do I get to her before Friday or catch her after the meeting, and what do I actually say? I don't want a speech, I want words I can use.

Four years now I've been working nights on the surgical recovery ward of a small public hospital in the Alentejo, and the whole time I've watched the same pattern repeat: people get sent home after operations with a stack of instructions they can't follow, nobody checks on them, and within a fortnight half of them are back in emergency with infected wounds or because they've stopped a medication they never understood. So I wrote up a plan for a daily nurse-led follow-up clinic with a paid specialist, someone who actually knows aftercare. I priced it out, I did the work properly. The woman who manages the hospital's accounts took me aside last week and told me, unofficially, that the board would never fund that — the most they'd accept is one afternoon a month, covered by existing nurses putting in unpaid extra hours, with anything beyond the basics sent on to the regional hospital two hours away. Which is close to what already happens, except with a booking list attached. The two nurses I run the discharge desk with have told me that if I put that version forward they'll read it as me abandoning the patients, because it'll look like help is coming and end with people being handed a phone number and a long wait. And honestly, I understand where they're standing. But the full plan has no chance at all. Not a slim chance — none. The budget isn't there and not one board member is pushing for it. So what's actually in front of me is a reduced service that at least operates, that in a year I can hold up and say, look, we turn people away every single month, now fund it properly — or nothing at all, just a document sitting on my laptop staying flawless while real patients keep bouncing back through our doors. My colleagues talk as though accepting the monthly version buries the real clinic permanently, but from where I stand the real clinic never existed to be buried. Nobody has given me a date to decide by, no one is making me submit it now — but no one else is going to carry this either. Am I kidding myself that getting something running counts for anything, or are they being purists about a plan that was dead before it was written? Do I put it to the board?
